tier_reason: Well-known independent third-party shootout (LesnyRumcajs/grpc_bench, 939 stars, MIT): the 2022-04-23 wiki page states the CPU (Xeon E5-1650 v3), benchmarked commit 14a8435 and settings, and the harness is public (cpp_grpc_mt_bench/main.cpp and Dockerfile, go_grpc_bench/Dockerfile, bench.sh). It falls short of A because the gRPC C++ library under test is Debian's prebuilt libgrpc++-dev pulled at image-build time: its version is neither stated nor pinned, and the Dockerfile's -O3 -flto only applies to the server glue and generated stubs.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: At the benchmarked commit 14a8435 (cpp_grpc_mt_bench/Dockerfile): FROM gcc:11, apt-get install libgrpc++-dev libjemalloc-dev, then g++ --std=c++20 -O3 -flto main.cpp gen/helloworld.grpc.pb.cc gen/helloworld.pb.cc -lgrpc++ -lprotobuf -lgrpc -lpthread -ljemalloc. The -O3 -flto flags apply only to the server code and generated stubs; the gRPC C++ core is Debian's prebuilt package (version not stated or pinned, built with Debian's flags). go_grpc built with golang:1.17 (go_grpc_bench/Dockerfile). Client: ghz image obvionaoe/ghz:v0.103.0.
corrections.caveats: Low confidence that gRPC C++ is faster than the baselines on current code. The record rests on an April 2022 run of the third-party grpc_bench shootout; the grpc/grpc README itself only links a performance dashboard and compares nothing. The shootout compares implementations of one protocol across languages, not gRPC against a different RPC system, and gRPC C++ is itself the category's usual incumbent. Neither the 2022 run nor the latest one measures a pinned gRPC release: cpp_grpc_mt links whatever libgrpc++-dev the Debian base of the gcc image ships (gcc:11 in 2022, gcc:15.2.0 at commit c4c93b3), so the measured library lags upstream gRPC; it also links jemalloc. The newest posted run (discussion 559, posted by maintainer LesnyRumcajs 2026-04-22, Intel Xeon Gold 6548N, commit c4c93b3, 11 client CPUs) reverses the result at 2-4 server CPUs: cpp_grpc_mt 74,574 req/s vs go_grpc 88,531 and java_hotspot_grpc_g1gc 96,459 at 2 CPUs; 81,581 vs 109,481 and 126,895 at 3 CPUs; 85,485 vs 117,082 and 131,958 at 4 CPUs, with Rust tonic, .NET, Scala and Java Vert.x also ahead. At 1 CPU in that run cpp_grpc_mt is roughly tied: 57,403 vs go_grpc 55,667 and java_hotspot_grpc_g1gc 57,291 (about 1.03x over Go, derived from page data), with the lowest p99 (21.81 ms vs 37.04 ms). In 2022 cpp_grpc_mt was slower than Go at 1 CPU (26,376 vs 34,289 req/s). The wins that hold in both runs are against the Python gRPC server (about 20x in 2022 at 2 CPUs, derived from page data) and lower memory than Java. The grpc_bench README warns that throughput rankings should be read together with CPU and memory use. awesome-cpp tags the licence as BSD; the repo is Apache-2.0. A Python REST-vs-gRPC coursework repo (MedhaRudra/REST-vs-gRPC) was opened by the search agent and not used: Python-only, no licence, its REST client opens a new TCP connection per query.

notes: All 2022 numbers (1/2/3-CPU rows for cpp_grpc_mt, go_grpc, java_hotspot_grpc_g1gc, python_grpc) match the wiki page exactly, and 9 client CPUs is confirmed. I opened discussion 559 and confirmed the record's reversal figures; I added the 3-CPU and 1-CPU rows and the Java HotSpot reversal to the caveats. Shortcomings to record: claim not reproduced by the newest run of the same harness (slower than go_grpc and grpc-java at 2-4 CPUs), gRPC library version unpinned (distro package), cross-language comparison of the same protocol rather than a faster alternative to an incumbent. Licence Apache-2.0, 45.4k stars, not archived; last commit date could not be re-checked (github.com commits page returned HTTP 429), so last_commit is left as recorded.

tier_reason: First-party example output in iceoryx_examples/iceperf/README.md compares iceoryx with POSIX message queues and Unix domain sockets and names the CPU (Xeon E3-1505M v5, Ubuntu 18.04). The harness is public (iceoryx_examples/iceperf: base.cpp, iceoryx.cpp, mq.cpp, uds.cpp), but the compiler, flags and build type are not stated and it is a single example run, so it stays C.

corrections.workload: iceperf example: leader and follower processes ping-pong 100000 round trips per payload size from 1 kB to 4096 kB (README run; the code default is 10000). The reported figure is one-way latency: total loop time divided by 2 x round trips (base.cpp). Timing covers loan/allocation, release and the send/receive calls only; the payload is never filled beyond a small header. All three transports busy-poll the receiver (nonblocking mq_receive / recvfrom loops, iceoryx take() loop). On Linux the message queue and Unix domain socket baselines send at most 4 kB per message (MAX_MESSAGE_SIZE in mq.hpp and uds.hpp), so a 4096 kB payload is split into 1024 messages per direction.
corrections.caveats: First-party example output from the README, a single run on a mobile Xeon under Ubuntu 18.04; compiler, flags and build type are not stated, so it stays C although the iceperf source is public. Latency is flat by construction: iceoryx passes a pointer into shared memory while the message queue and Unix domain socket must copy the payload through the kernel, and the timing excludes filling and reading the payload, so it is not an end-to-end application figure. The baselines are also handicapped at large sizes: in the current harness both are capped at 4 kB per message on Linux (message queue depth 8), so a 4096 kB payload becomes 1024 syscall-level sends and receives each way, and each baseline send heap-allocates a payload-sized buffer inside the timed loop. The 2,000x-2,800x large-payload ratios therefore mostly reflect fragmentation plus copying, not a tuned baseline; the 1 kB ratios (about 4x and 6x) are the fairer figure. All three transports busy-poll, so wake-up latency of a blocking receiver is not measured. The Unix domain socket baseline is nonblocking SOCK_DGRAM; its sender retries on ENOBUFS/EAGAIN without sleeping (the 10 ms retry sleep is only in the connection handshake, outside the timing). No comparison with other shared-memory IPC (Boost.Interprocess, ZeroMQ ipc, Cyclone DDS shm). The repo page says iceoryx classic is in maintenance mode with only security fixes, iceoryx2 being the successor; the repo now carries a SECURITY.md.

notes: README numbers match the record exactly (iceoryx C++ and C API rows are identical). I read the harness: latency is one-way (round trip / 2), all transports busy-poll, and the MQ/UDS baselines fragment payloads into 4 kB messages and allocate a buffer per send, which inflates the large-payload ratios; the record's claim that the UDS sender sleeps between retries was wrong and is corrected. Shortcomings to record: example output only (no compiler/flags), large-payload ratios inflated by 4 kB baseline fragmentation, not end-to-end, maintenance mode. Category websocket-grpc-rpc is a loose fit for shared-memory IPC middleware; the last commit date could not be re-checked (commits page HTTP 429), so it is left as recorded.
